what_its_for: This medicine helps your body make more white blood cells after you receive chemotherapy. Chemotherapy can lower your white blood cell count, which makes it harder for your body to fight infections. Eflapegrastim-xnst helps reduce your risk of getting a serious infection called febrile neutropenia, which is a fever caused by having too few white blood cells.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) under your skin, usually in your upper arm, stomach area, or thigh. A healthcare provider will give you this injection. It comes as a pre-filled syringe. Do NOT inject it into skin that is sore, red, bruised, or scarred. Each pre-filled syringe is for one-time use only — never reuse a syringe.
dosing: You will typically receive one injection of 13.2 mg once per chemotherapy cycle. Your doctor will give you the shot at least 24 hours AFTER your chemotherapy treatment. Do not receive this shot within 14 days BEFORE your next chemotherapy cycle. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions about when to get your injection.
missed_dose: If you miss your scheduled injection appointment, call your doctor or healthcare provider right away to reschedule. It is very important to get this shot after each chemotherapy cycle to protect you from serious infections. Do not try to give yourself this injection at home unless your doctor has specifically trained you and instructed you to do so.
storage: Store this medicine in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it in its original packaging to protect it from light. Do NOT freeze it — if it accidentally freezes, throw it away and get a new one. Do not shake the syringe. If needed, you may keep it at room temperature (up to 77°F / 25°C) for no more than 12 hours. Throw away any unused medicine — do not save it for later use.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive this injection within 14 days before starting a new chemotherapy cycle or within 24 hours after receiving chemotherapy. Avoid pressing on the injection site excessively after the shot. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines while on this medicine. Avoid activities that may cause injury to your bones, as this medicine can rarely cause a serious bone condition.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor immediately or go to the emergency room if you experience: a high fever (100.4°F / 38°C or higher), chills, or signs of infection; severe bone or muscle pain that does not get better with over-the-counter pain medicines; pain in the left upper side of your belly or left shoulder (this could be a sign of a spleen problem); sudden shortness of breath, trouble breathing, or your lips or skin turn bluish (signs of a lung problem); unusual swelling in your hands, feet, or face; very fast heartbeat; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working fairly quickly after your injection to signal your body to produce more white blood cells. Your white blood cell count will usually begin to rise within 1 to 2 days and reach its peak within about 3 to 4 days after your injection. Your doctor may check your blood counts during your treatment to make sure the medicine is working properly.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known whether this medicine can harm an unborn baby or pass into breast milk. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your doctor may need to monitor you more closely. Children: The safety and effectiveness of this medicine in children has not been established. Sickle cell disease: If you have sickle cell disease, tell your doctor before using this medicine, as it may trigger a sickle cell crisis.
